summary.text: Phospholipids are lipids whose molecules have a hydrophilic head containing a phosphate group and two hydrophobic tails derived from fatty acids.
Because they are amphiphilic, they can form lipid bilayers, the dominant structural motif of the membranes of all cells.
In eukaryotes, sterols are interspersed among them, and the combination gives fluidity in two dimensions with mechanical strength against rupture.

facts.value: Lecithin in chicken egg yolk, by Theodore Gobley in 1847

facts.label: Basic shape
facts.value: One hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails

facts.label: Head modifications
facts.value: The phosphate can carry choline, ethanolamine or serine

facts.value: On the cytosolic side of the ER membrane

facts.label: Drug delivery
facts.value: Used to prepare liposomal and other nanoformulations of drugs

items.prompt: Phospholipids are dropped into a watery solution. What arrangement tends to form?

options.label: A bilayer, with tails inside and heads facing the liquid
A single layer, with heads pointing inward
A bilayer, with heads inside and tails facing the liquid
A loose tangle with no repeating arrangement

items.explain: Driven by hydrophobic interactions, they form a bilayer with heads exposed to the liquid on both sides and tails directed into the membrane.

items.prompt: Eukaryotic membranes mix a second class of lipid among their phospholipids. What does the combination give the membrane?

options.label: Rigidity in all directions, so nothing can move
Fluidity only, with no resistance to rupture
Two-dimensional fluidity plus strength against rupture
The protection of a thick cell wall

items.explain: Sterols interspersed among phospholipids provide fluidity in two dimensions combined with mechanical strength against rupture.

items.prompt: A textbook pictures the membrane as a mosaic where proteins and lipids drift sideways freely. How well does that picture hold up?

options.label: Every new technique has confirmed it in full
It has been superseded, as lipid behaviour is not simple
It applies only to the nuclear membrane
Later work showed that proteins never move at all

items.explain: The fluid mosaic model has been superseded, because the behaviour of lipids under physiological conditions is not simple.

items.prompt: One end of a phospholipid is drawn to water and the other end avoids it. What word describes this?

options.label: Hydrophobic
Hydrophilic
Birefringent
Amphiphilic

items.explain: Phospholipids are amphiphilic, with a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails.

items.prompt: Where in the cell do the proteins that build phospholipids sit?

options.label: Inside the nucleus on the chromosomes
On the outer surface of the cell membrane
On the cytosol-facing side of the ER membrane
Within the matrix of the mitochondria

items.explain: Phospholipid synthesis occurs on the cytosolic side of the ER membrane, which is studded with the proteins for synthesis and allocation.

paragraphs.heading: A molecule with two ends
paragraphs.text: Phospholipids are a family of lipids built in two parts: a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails. The head holds a phosphate group joined to an alcohol, most often glycerol, which links it to the tails. The tails come from fatty acids. Small organic molecules such as choline, ethanolamine or serine can be attached to the phosphate.

paragraphs.heading: Water-loving and water-shy
paragraphs.text: Because one end faces water and the other avoids it, phospholipids are called amphiphilic. The hydrophilic end usually carries a phosphate group with a negative charge. The hydrophobic end is usually a pair of long fatty acid chains. Put many phospholipids into water and the tails crowd together, keeping their contact with the water as small as they can.

paragraphs.heading: The bilayer
paragraphs.text: That crowding often produces a bilayer: a sheet two molecules thick. The two layers face opposite ways, so heads sit on both outer surfaces in the water while the tails point inward, toward each other. Their amphiphilic nature is what lets phospholipids form this sheet. It is the main building plan for the membranes of every cell, and for some other structures such as vesicles and virus coatings.

paragraphs.heading: Partners in the membrane
paragraphs.text: In real membranes, phospholipids often share the bilayer with proteins, glycolipids and sterols. In eukaryotes, sterols are scattered among the phospholipids and stop them from packing tightly together, which helps keep the membrane fluid. The mix gives a membrane that can flow within its own plane yet resists bursting. The fluid mosaic model pictured the membrane as a sea of lipids through which proteins and lipids drift sideways. That model has since been replaced, as later study showed lipid behaviour is not that simple.

paragraphs.heading: Where cells make them
paragraphs.text: Cells build phospholipids on the cytosol-facing side of the ER membrane. Proteins set in that membrane do the work: acyl transferases, a phosphatase and choline phosphotransferase assemble the molecules, while flippase and floppase sort them. Later a vesicle buds off from the ER. Its outer layer carries phospholipids bound for the cytoplasmic side of the cell membrane, and its inner layer carries those bound for the exoplasmic side.

paragraphs.heading: Egg yolk to medicine
paragraphs.text: The first phospholipid recognised in living tissue was lecithin, also called phosphatidylcholine. The French chemist and pharmacist Theodore Nicolas Gobley found it in chicken egg yolk in 1847. Today purified phospholipids are made commercially for nanotechnology and materials science. They are also used to package drugs into liposomes and other nano-sized formulations, which can raise a drug's bio-availability, cut its toxicity or help it cross membranes. Liposomes are often made from phospholipids rich in phosphatidylcholine.
